lesson.menu_title: What Really Happened — Putting the Emphasis Where You Want It

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- What Really Happened
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 4 -- What Really Happened

listenings.text: Good afternoon. I want to set out what we know one week on. At eleven minutes past two on Tuesday morning, an alarm was recorded at the substation. At fourteen minutes past two, the main transformer disconnected, and within six minutes approximately four hundred thousand customers had lost supply. The cause, on the evidence available to us today, was a storm of a severity that this equipment was not designed to withstand. I am aware that questions have been raised about the interval between the alarm and the disconnection, and that interval is being reviewed. A full report will be published within ninety days. Nothing will be withheld from it. I will take three questions.

The log is not complicated. It is one page. There was an inspection due the previous March, and it was postponed, and then it was postponed again, and then it simply is not there any more. I raised it twice. I was told it was a scheduling matter and not my department, which, I mean, technically that is correct. And I let it go, and that is the part I think about. What I still cannot tell you, two years on, is who took it off the calendar. The system that would have recorded that was replaced in January, and nobody kept the old one. So the honest answer is that we know what happened and we do not know who decided it, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.

extra_audio.text: Priya says the hardest part of an inquiry is deciding which question you are answering. He suggests the question looked obvious from outside: why the city went dark. She replies that the real question was why nine minutes passed between the alarm and the disconnection. She admits that she signed the page which downplayed the discrepancy in one line. She explains that an engineer nobody was listening to kept insisting the statement did not square with the recording.

paras: What is beyond dispute is this. At 02:11 on a Tuesday in March an alarm sounded at a substation on the edge of the city. At 02:14 the main transformer disconnected. By 02:20 four hundred thousand people were without power, and it was nine hours before the last of them had it back. Nobody has ever argued about those four sentences.

The first account, published within a week, blamed the weather. It was a storm, the statement said, of a severity the equipment had not been designed for. That version held for eleven months, largely because the inquiry took the operator at his word and because there was no reason not to. What it did not explain was the nine-minute discrepancy between the alarm and the disconnection, and the report downplayed it in a single line.

What changed everything was a maintenance log that came to light in the second year. It showed that a routine inspection scheduled for the previous March had been postponed twice and then quietly removed from the calendar. Two engineers corroborated it independently. The storm, in the event, turned out to be a red herring: it was the postponed inspection, not the weather, that was at the heart of the whole sequence.

The final report is careful about what it does not know. Three loose ends are listed on the last page, and one of them still matters: nobody can say who removed the inspection from the calendar, or why. The reason why that question survived two years is not a conspiracy. It is that the system which recorded the decision was replaced in January, and to all intents and purposes the record no longer exists.
